flashcards.back: A model for enabling ubiquitous, convenient, on-demand network access to a shared pool of configurable computing resources that can be rapidly provisioned and released with minimal management effort or provider interaction.
flashcards.detail: The NIST definition lists five essential characteristics, three service models and four deployment models; the exam expects you to reason from it, not just recite it.

flashcards.back: On-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity and measured service (NIST). ISO/IEC 17788 names the same ideas plus multi-tenancy and scalability.
flashcards.detail: If a service lacks self-service provisioning or metering, it is virtualized hosting rather than true cloud; scenario questions test that distinction.

flashcards.back: Several customers (tenants) share the same physical and logical resources while the provider keeps their data and workloads logically isolated from one another.
flashcards.detail: It is the economic engine of cloud and also its signature risk: a failure of isolation exposes one tenant to another.

flashcards.back: The provider supplies compute, storage and networking as virtualized resources; the customer installs and manages operating systems, middleware, applications and data on top.
flashcards.detail: The customer owns the most security work in IaaS: guest OS patching, network rules, identity and data protection are all theirs.

flashcards.back: The provider runs the infrastructure, operating system and runtime; the customer deploys and manages only their own applications and data.
flashcards.detail: Responsibility shifts up the stack, but the customer still owns application code, configuration, identities and data.

flashcards.back: The provider delivers a complete application over the network; the customer configures it and supplies users and data but manages none of the underlying stack.
flashcards.detail: Even in SaaS the customer always keeps accountability for their data, user access and acceptable-use settings.

flashcards.back: The division of security duties between provider and customer. The provider secures the cloud itself (facilities, hardware, hypervisor, core services); the customer secures what they put in and how they configure it. The split moves with the service model.
flashcards.detail: The most-tested concept in the domain; the safe default is that data, identities and customer-side configuration are always the customer's problem.

flashcards.front: Public, private, hybrid and community cloud
flashcards.back: Public: provider-owned and open to many customers. Private: dedicated to one organization. Hybrid: two or more models bound together so data and workloads can move. Community: shared by organizations with common requirements such as a regulator.
flashcards.detail: Multi-cloud (several providers) is not the same as hybrid; watch for questions that test that difference.

flashcards.back: Using services from two or more cloud providers, often for resilience, best-of-breed services or negotiating leverage.
flashcards.detail: It multiplies skills, identity, logging and policy-consistency work, and is a stated focus of the newer CCSP outline.

flashcards.front: Cloud service customer, provider, partner and broker
flashcards.back: ISO/IEC 17788 roles: the customer consumes services; the provider delivers them; a partner supports either side (for example an auditor, developer or broker); a cloud service broker intermediates, aggregates or customizes services.
flashcards.detail: Questions ask who bears accountability for a given duty; a broker or reseller never removes the customer's accountability.

flashcards.back: An independent party that assesses a provider's controls and conformance to standards, producing assurance that customers and regulators can rely on.
flashcards.detail: Customers rarely audit hyperscale providers directly; they rely on independent reports such as SOC 2 and ISO certifications.

flashcards.back: A dependency on one provider's proprietary services, formats or APIs that makes moving elsewhere costly or technically hard.
flashcards.detail: Mitigate with portability, open standards, exit plans and contract clauses; tested together with reversibility.

flashcards.back: Portability: moving workloads or data between providers with minimal change. Interoperability: different systems working together. Reversibility: the customer can retrieve their assets and have the provider delete the rest on exit.
flashcards.detail: All three are cross-cutting cloud aspects and drive exit-strategy and contract questions.

flashcards.back: Scalability is the ability to handle growing load by adding capacity; elasticity is the automatic, rapid adding and releasing of capacity to match demand.
flashcards.detail: Elastic implies automatic and both ways (shrink as well as grow); a manual upgrade is only scalable.

flashcards.back: The provider combines its computing resources to serve many customers from a shared pool, dynamically assigning and reassigning capacity by demand.
flashcards.detail: It underpins multi-tenancy; the customer typically has no control over exact physical location beyond region or zone.

flashcards.back: Resource usage is monitored, controlled and reported so it can be billed and optimized, giving transparency to both sides.
flashcards.detail: The same metering feeds cost-based attacks: stolen credentials used for crypto-mining show up as a spike in usage.

flashcards.back: ISO/IEC 17789 lists concerns that apply across the architecture: auditability, availability, governance, interoperability, maintenance and versioning, performance, portability, privacy, regulatory, resiliency, reversibility, security and service levels.
flashcards.detail: Use them as a checklist when a scenario asks what an architect must consider before adopting a service.

flashcards.back: Running a workload in a private environment and overflowing to a public cloud when demand exceeds local capacity.
flashcards.detail: A hybrid pattern whose risks are data exposure in the burst environment and network latency between the two.

flashcards.front: Cloud security principles: defense in depth, least privilege and zero trust
flashcards.back: Layer independent controls so one failure is not fatal; grant only the access required; and never trust a request because of its network location, verifying identity and context every time.
flashcards.detail: Cloud has no trusted perimeter, so identity becomes the new perimeter; exam answers favor layered, identity-centric designs.

flashcards.back: Protecting data while it is being processed by running workloads inside a hardware-based trusted execution environment (TEE) whose memory is encrypted and isolated even from the host and provider administrators.
flashcards.detail: It closes the gap that at-rest and in-transit encryption leave open (data in use) and is named in the outline's treatment of related technologies.

flashcards.front: Artificial intelligence and machine learning as cloud workloads
flashcards.back: Cloud platforms provide managed training, inference and model-hosting services, so training data, models and prompts become assets that need classification, access control and provenance tracking.
flashcards.detail: The newer outline weaves AI and ML security into every domain; expect shared-responsibility and data-protection angles, not deep model mathematics.

flashcards.back: Processing data near where it is produced (devices, branches or local nodes) rather than in a central cloud region, to reduce latency and bandwidth.
flashcards.detail: It widens the attack surface with many physically exposed nodes that need identity, patching and remote attestation.

flashcards.front: Quantum computing risk and post-quantum cryptography
flashcards.back: A large-scale quantum computer could break public-key algorithms such as RSA and elliptic-curve schemes, so data that must stay secret for years is exposed to harvest-now, decrypt-later collection. Post-quantum algorithms are being standardized as the answer.
flashcards.detail: Architects plan crypto agility: the ability to swap algorithms without redesigning systems.

flashcards.back: A tamper-evident ledger replicated across many parties, with entries chained by cryptographic hashes. Cloud providers offer it as a managed service.
flashcards.detail: It gives integrity and auditability, not confidentiality; do not store regulated personal data on an immutable ledger that cannot honor deletion.

flashcards.back: Networked physical devices that sense or act, often resource-constrained and long-lived, feeding data to cloud back ends.
flashcards.detail: Weak default credentials and no patch path are the usual findings; the cloud side needs device identity, certificate lifecycle and ingestion limits.

flashcards.back: A vendor-neutral model (ISO/IEC 17789 and NIST SP 500-292) describing actors, activities and functional layers of cloud computing so designs and controls can be compared consistently.
flashcards.detail: Use it to locate where a control belongs: user, access, services, resources or cross-cutting layer.

flashcards.back: The contract component stating measurable service targets such as availability, support response and remedies when the provider misses them.
flashcards.detail: SLA credits compensate cost, not business loss; resilience still needs customer-side architecture.

flashcards.back: Create, store, use, share, archive and destroy: the six phases data passes through, each needing its own controls and ownership. Data can move between phases in any direction over time.
flashcards.detail: Tests ask which control fits which phase, for example classification at create and verified destruction at the end.

flashcards.back: Labeling data by sensitivity and business impact (for example public, internal, confidential, restricted) so that handling, encryption, access and retention rules can be applied consistently.
flashcards.detail: Classification is the first step; without it every later control is a guess. The data owner assigns it.

flashcards.back: Finding where sensitive data actually lives, using content inspection, pattern matching, labels and machine learning, across structured, unstructured and semi-structured stores.
flashcards.detail: Cloud sprawl and shadow IT mean you cannot protect what you have not found; discovery precedes classification and DLP.

flashcards.back: The owner is accountable for the data and decides classification and access; the steward manages quality and rules day to day; the custodian operates the systems that hold it. In cloud the provider is typically a custodian or processor.
flashcards.detail: Accountability cannot be delegated to the provider even though custody can.

flashcards.back: The controller decides why and how personal data is processed and carries primary legal responsibility; the processor handles it on the controller's behalf under contract.
flashcards.detail: In most cloud scenarios the customer is the controller and the provider is the processor; sub-processors extend the chain.

flashcards.back: Structured data fits a fixed schema (relational tables); unstructured has no model (documents, images, email); semi-structured carries tags but no rigid schema (JSON, XML).
flashcards.detail: Discovery and DLP are hardest on unstructured data, which is most of what organizations hold.

flashcards.back: Controls that discover, monitor and block the unauthorized movement of sensitive data across endpoints, networks and cloud services, using content and context rules.
flashcards.detail: DLP depends on classification and discovery; encrypted traffic needs inspection points that can see the content.

flashcards.back: Persistent protection that travels with a file, enforcing who may open, copy, print or forward it, and allowing access to be revoked after sharing.
flashcards.detail: Best answer when the requirement is control of a document after it leaves your environment; DLP only controls egress.

flashcards.back: Rules for how long each class of data must be kept and when it must be disposed of, driven by legal, regulatory and business needs.
flashcards.detail: Keep too little and you violate law; keep too much and you enlarge breach and eDiscovery exposure.

flashcards.back: A directive suspending normal deletion of data that may be relevant to litigation or investigation until counsel releases it.
flashcards.detail: Overrides retention schedules; cloud lifecycle and auto-delete rules must be able to honor it.

flashcards.back: Because customers cannot physically destroy provider media, cloud destruction relies on cryptographic erasure: encrypt the data and destroy every copy of the key, rendering the data unrecoverable.
flashcards.detail: The standard cloud answer to 'how do you guarantee deletion'; it works only if keys are truly isolated and destroyed.

flashcards.back: Breaking data into fragments and spreading them across multiple locations or providers (as erasure coding does) so no single location holds usable data and availability improves.
flashcards.detail: Improves durability and resilience but complicates data residency and deletion tracking.

flashcards.front: Data flows and data flow diagrams
flashcards.back: A map of where data enters, moves, is processed, stored and leaves a system, including across providers and regions.
flashcards.detail: Required to find trust boundaries, apply residency rules and answer regulator questions; a first step in cloud risk work.

flashcards.front: Data lake and AI training dataset security
flashcards.back: Large central repositories and curated datasets used for analytics and model training need classification, fine-grained access control, lineage tracking and protection against tampering, since poisoned data corrupts every model trained on it.
flashcards.detail: Newer outline content: integrity and provenance of training data matter as much as confidentiality.

flashcards.back: Replacing sensitive values with realistic but non-sensitive ones (static masking in copies, dynamic masking at query time) so non-production use does not expose real data.
flashcards.detail: Masking can be irreversible, unlike tokenization; the best test-data answer when real values are not needed.

flashcards.back: Anonymization irreversibly removes the link to an individual so data is no longer personal data; pseudonymization replaces identifiers with a separate key or mapping, so data remains personal data under privacy law.
flashcards.detail: Pseudonymized data is still regulated under GDPR; truly anonymized data is not. Re-identification risk is the tested trap.

flashcards.back: Attaching metadata such as classification, owner and retention class to data and cloud resources so policies and automation can act on them.
flashcards.detail: Labels make DLP, access policy and billing work at scale; unlabeled assets are the gap attackers and auditors find.

flashcards.back: Object storage holds data as objects with metadata over APIs; block storage provides raw volumes for VMs and databases; file storage offers shared file systems. Ephemeral storage disappears with the instance.
flashcards.detail: Each type has different encryption, access and exposure risks; public object buckets are the classic misconfiguration.

flashcards.back: Tools that observe database queries and changes in real time, flagging or blocking suspicious access and producing audit trails independent of the database's own logs.
flashcards.detail: A detective control for privileged-user abuse; useful where native logging is limited or tamper-prone.

flashcards.front: Encryption at rest, in transit and in use
flashcards.back: At rest protects stored data, in transit protects data crossing a network (for example TLS) and in use protects data while processed (confidential computing). A complete strategy covers all three.
flashcards.detail: Pick the answer that matches the state of data in the scenario; one control rarely covers all three.

flashcards.back: Symmetric uses one shared secret key and is fast, suiting bulk data; asymmetric uses a public and private key pair and is slower, suiting key exchange, signatures and identity.
flashcards.detail: Real systems combine them: asymmetric to exchange or wrap a symmetric key that protects the bulk data.

flashcards.back: A data encryption key (DEK) encrypts the data; a key encryption key (KEK) held in a key management service encrypts the DEK. Rotating or revoking the KEK controls many DEKs cheaply.
flashcards.detail: The default design in cloud storage and database services; crypto-shredding works by destroying the KEK.

flashcards.back: A managed service that creates, stores, rotates, controls access to and audits use of cryptographic keys, integrated with the provider's other services.
flashcards.detail: Convenient and the default, but the provider operates it unless you add stronger options such as BYOK or HYOK.

flashcards.back: A tamper-resistant device that generates and stores keys and performs cryptographic operations without exposing the keys; validated to standards such as FIPS 140.
flashcards.detail: Choose an HSM (or cloud HSM) when policy demands hardware-protected, single-tenant key custody.

flashcards.back: The customer generates the key material and imports it into the provider's KMS or HSM, keeping an original copy and the ability to revoke or delete it.
flashcards.detail: More control than provider-generated keys, but the provider still uses the key to decrypt on your behalf.

flashcards.back: The customer keeps keys entirely outside the provider, for example in an on-premises HSM, so the provider can never decrypt the data and services that need plaintext may not work.
flashcards.detail: Strongest separation of duties, with trade-offs in availability, latency and feature support.

flashcards.back: Generation, distribution, storage, use, rotation, revocation, archival and destruction. Weakness at any stage undermines the encryption built on the key.
flashcards.detail: Know the order and the control at each step; poorly protected key storage and absent rotation are the common failures.

flashcards.back: Keys should be stored apart from the data they protect and managed by different administrators than the data owners; escrow places a copy with a trusted third party for recovery.
flashcards.detail: Storing keys beside data in the same account defeats encryption; escrow introduces its own exposure that must be justified.

flashcards.back: Substituting sensitive data with a random surrogate token while the real value sits in a secured vault; the token has no mathematical relationship to the original.
flashcards.detail: Reduces compliance scope (for example for card data) because systems holding only tokens never touch the real value.

flashcards.back: A hash is a one-way fixed-length fingerprint for integrity checks; a digital signature signs a hash with a private key to prove origin, integrity and non-repudiation.
flashcards.detail: Hashing is not encryption and is not reversible; salted hashes protect stored passwords.

flashcards.back: The protocol that provides confidentiality, integrity and server authentication for data in transit using certificates; TLS 1.3 is the current version and removes legacy weaknesses.
flashcards.detail: Prefer TLS 1.2 or higher with strong suites; disable legacy SSL and early TLS.

flashcards.front: Public key infrastructure (PKI) and certificate lifecycle
flashcards.back: The roles, policies and services (certificate authorities, registration, revocation) that bind public keys to identities and manage certificates from issuance to expiry.
flashcards.detail: Expired or unrevoked certificates cause outages and exposure; automate renewal and monitor transparency logs.

flashcards.back: Encryption that allows computation directly on ciphertext, yielding an encrypted result that decrypts to the correct output, so data stays protected while processed.
flashcards.detail: Powerful but computationally expensive; an answer for data in use when enclaves are not acceptable.

flashcards.back: Designing systems so cryptographic algorithms, key lengths and libraries can be replaced quickly without redesigning applications.
flashcards.detail: Directly addresses post-quantum migration and deprecated algorithm risk.

flashcards.back: Provider-managed keys are created, rotated and held by the provider by default; customer-managed keys are controlled by the customer in KMS or HSM with their own policies, rotation and revocation, while the provider's service still performs the cryptography.
flashcards.detail: Customer-managed keys mean the customer controls revocation; they are not the same as HYOK.

flashcards.back: Central storage, rotation and audited access for non-human credentials such as API keys, passwords and certificates, injected at runtime rather than embedded in code or images.
flashcards.detail: Hard-coded secrets in repositories and container images are among the most frequent real-world cloud breaches.

flashcards.back: A Type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisor runs directly on hardware and underpins cloud platforms; a Type 2 (hosted) hypervisor runs as an application on a host operating system and is mostly used on workstations.
flashcards.detail: A hypervisor compromise exposes every guest on the host, so hardening and patching it is the provider's top priority.

flashcards.back: An attack in which code inside a guest virtual machine breaks isolation and reaches the hypervisor or other guests.
flashcards.detail: The canonical multi-tenancy threat; mitigations are patching, minimal hypervisor features and placing very sensitive workloads on dedicated hosts.

flashcards.back: Shared hardware lets one tenant infer secrets from another through timing, cache or resource-contention effects, or degrade a neighbor's performance by consuming shared resources.
flashcards.detail: Mitigate with dedicated hosts, resource quotas and confidential computing for the most sensitive workloads.

flashcards.back: Containers share the host kernel and are separated by namespaces and control groups; this is lighter than a virtual machine but a weaker isolation boundary.
flashcards.detail: A kernel flaw can affect every container on the host; sensitive multi-tenant workloads may need VM-level isolation.

flashcards.back: Build images from trusted minimal base images, scan for vulnerabilities and embedded secrets, sign them and pull only from a trusted registry, and rebuild rather than patching running containers.
flashcards.detail: Shift-left scanning plus admission control that refuses unsigned or vulnerable images is the standard answer.

flashcards.back: Role-based access control for the API server, network policies between pods, pod security standards, secrets protection, admission controllers and an audit log of control-plane activity.
flashcards.detail: The control plane and kubelet APIs are the crown jewels; an exposed dashboard or over-privileged service account is the usual breach.

flashcards.back: Code runs in short-lived, provider-managed execution environments triggered by events, with no servers for the customer to patch.
flashcards.detail: Risks shift to over-privileged function roles, insecure event inputs, vulnerable dependencies and poor visibility; apply least privilege per function.

flashcards.back: A logically isolated virtual network in a public cloud, divided into subnets (public or private) with route tables controlling whether traffic can reach the internet.
flashcards.detail: Place data tiers in private subnets with no direct internet route; public exposure should be a deliberate exception.

flashcards.back: Security groups are stateful rules attached to instances or interfaces; network access control lists are stateless rules applied at the subnet boundary and evaluated in order.
flashcards.detail: Stateful means return traffic is allowed automatically; stateless rules need both directions defined.

flashcards.back: Applying fine-grained policy between individual workloads or tiers so a compromised host cannot move freely to its neighbors.
flashcards.detail: The cloud answer to lateral movement; it replaces coarse network zones with identity- or tag-based rules.

flashcards.back: Separating the network control plane from the data plane so networks are configured programmatically through APIs rather than device by device.
flashcards.detail: Enables automation and consistent policy but makes the management API a high-value target.

flashcards.back: Granting access to specific applications per session based on verified user, device and context, instead of placing users on a broad network through a traditional VPN.
flashcards.detail: Preferred over network-level VPN access for remote users when the stem stresses least privilege.

flashcards.back: Dedicated links or VPN tunnels join on-premises networks to the cloud, and private endpoints expose a cloud service on a private address so traffic never traverses the public internet.
flashcards.detail: A dedicated link is private but not automatically encrypted; add encryption if the data requires it.

flashcards.back: Provider and third-party services absorb or scrub volumetric and application-layer floods using large capacity, anycast routing and rate limiting.
flashcards.detail: Elasticity helps, but unmetered scaling during an attack can become an economic denial of service; set budgets and alerts.

flashcards.back: Servers and containers are never modified after deployment; changes are made by building a new image and replacing the old instances.
flashcards.detail: Removes configuration drift and makes rollback and forensics simpler; patching means redeploying.

flashcards.back: Defining infrastructure in version-controlled templates that are reviewed, scanned for misconfiguration and enforced with policy as code before deployment.
flashcards.detail: A misconfigured template replicates a flaw at scale; scanning in the pipeline is cheaper than finding it in production.

flashcards.back: A trusted platform module and secure or measured boot verify the integrity of firmware and boot components, and remote attestation lets a service confirm a host's state before trusting it.
flashcards.detail: Underpins confidential computing and trustworthy workload placement.

flashcards.back: Resilient facilities use redundant power, cooling and connectivity (for example N+1 or 2N), physical access control and environmental monitoring, and are evaluated against recognized tier or standards frameworks.
flashcards.detail: Customers cannot inspect hyperscale sites, so they rely on independent audit reports and certification evidence.

flashcards.back: The console, APIs and command-line tools used to create, configure and delete cloud resources.
flashcards.detail: Compromise of management-plane credentials is catastrophic; protect it with multi-factor authentication, least privilege and detailed audit logging.

flashcards.front: Business continuity, disaster recovery and BCDR planning
flashcards.back: Business continuity keeps critical functions running through disruption; disaster recovery restores IT systems after a disaster; BCDR planning addresses both together.
flashcards.detail: DR is a subset of continuity; start from business impact analysis, not from technology.

flashcards.back: A structured assessment of how the loss of each process affects the organization over time, producing criticality rankings and recovery targets.
flashcards.detail: Recovery objectives must come from the BIA; choosing technology first is a classic wrong answer.

flashcards.back: The maximum acceptable time to restore a service after an outage.
flashcards.detail: A smaller RTO demands more expensive, more automated recovery options.

flashcards.back: The maximum acceptable amount of data loss measured in time, determining how often data must be replicated or backed up.
flashcards.detail: RPO drives backup and replication frequency; RTO drives the recovery architecture.

flashcards.back: The longest an organization can lose a function before the harm becomes unacceptable, which sets an upper bound above the RTO.
flashcards.detail: RTO must be shorter than the maximum tolerable downtime or recovery will arrive too late.

flashcards.back: A region is a geographic area; availability zones are isolated data-center groups within it. Spreading across zones tolerates a facility failure, spreading across regions tolerates a regional disaster.
flashcards.detail: Match the design to the failure scenario and to data residency constraints.

flashcards.back: In increasing cost and speed: backup and restore, pilot light (minimal core running), warm standby (scaled-down copy) and active-active (full capacity in more than one location).
flashcards.detail: Pick the cheapest option that meets the stated RTO and RPO.

flashcards.back: Synchronous replication commits to both sites before acknowledging, giving near-zero data loss but adding latency; asynchronous acknowledges first and copies later, performing better over distance but risking some data loss.
flashcards.detail: A near-zero RPO across long distances usually conflicts with performance; know the trade-off.

flashcards.back: Backups that cannot be altered or deleted for a retention period, or are logically separated from production credentials, so ransomware or an attacker cannot destroy them.
flashcards.detail: The key defense against ransomware; test restores, not just backups.

flashcards.back: Identifying assets, threats and vulnerabilities in a cloud design, estimating likelihood and impact and choosing treatment. Typical cloud risks include loss of governance, isolation failure, insecure interfaces, management-plane compromise and vendor lock-in.
flashcards.detail: Risk analysis precedes control selection, and the owner of the asset accepts residual risk.

flashcards.back: Deliberately injecting failures, from game-day exercises to automated experiments, to confirm that failover, alerting and recovery procedures really work.
flashcards.detail: An untested plan is an assumption; tabletop, simulation and full failover tests are increasing in realism and risk.

flashcards.back: Building security activities into every phase of development: requirements, design, coding, testing, deployment and maintenance, rather than testing for security only at the end.
flashcards.detail: The earlier a defect is found the cheaper it is to fix; 'shift left' is the standard exam answer.

flashcards.back: Integrating security checks, automation and shared ownership into continuous integration and delivery pipelines so security keeps pace with frequent releases.
flashcards.detail: Automated scanning gates and policy as code replace slow manual security sign-offs.

flashcards.back: A structured method to find threats during design. STRIDE categorizes them as Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service and Elevation of privilege.
flashcards.detail: Do it at design time, using data flow diagrams and trust boundaries; know which STRIDE category matches which attack.

flashcards.back: PASTA is a risk-centric, seven-stage threat modeling process tied to business impact; attack trees decompose an attacker's goal into the steps needed to reach it.
flashcards.detail: Other models alongside STRIDE; the exam asks you to match method to purpose, not to run them in detail.

flashcards.back: A regularly updated awareness list of the most critical web application security risks, such as broken access control, injection and cryptographic failures.
flashcards.detail: It is a list of risk categories, not a standard to certify against; broken access control tops recent editions.

flashcards.back: Analyzing source code or binaries without running them to find coding flaws early in development.
flashcards.detail: Early and cheap but produces false positives and cannot see runtime or configuration issues.

flashcards.back: Testing a running application from the outside by sending crafted requests to find exploitable behavior.
flashcards.detail: Finds runtime and configuration flaws without source access; needs a deployed environment and is later in the cycle.

flashcards.front: Interactive application security testing (IAST) and runtime application self-protection (RASP)
flashcards.back: IAST instruments a running application during testing to report vulnerabilities with code context; RASP embeds protection inside the application to detect and block attacks at runtime.
flashcards.detail: IAST is a testing technique; RASP is a runtime defense. Do not confuse them with SAST and DAST.

flashcards.back: SCA finds known vulnerabilities and license issues in third-party libraries; a software bill of materials lists every component in a build so exposure can be assessed quickly when a flaw is announced.
flashcards.detail: Most modern applications are mostly third-party code, so supply-chain visibility is a core cloud application control.

flashcards.back: Protecting the code, dependencies, build systems and artifacts that produce software, using signed commits and artifacts, provenance records, locked dependency versions and hardened build pipelines.
flashcards.detail: Attackers target build pipelines and public packages; signing and provenance prove an artifact came from your trusted build.

flashcards.back: Securing programmatic interfaces with strong authentication and authorization on every call, input and schema validation, rate limiting, encryption in transit and an API gateway that centralizes policy.
flashcards.detail: Broken object-level authorization is the leading API risk; inventory shadow and deprecated APIs.

flashcards.back: A filter in front of web applications that inspects HTTP traffic and blocks common attacks such as injection and cross-site scripting.
flashcards.detail: A compensating control that buys time; it does not replace fixing the vulnerable code.

flashcards.back: Treat all input as untrusted, validate it against an allow-list, and encode output for its context so injected content is displayed as data rather than executed.
flashcards.detail: The root fix for injection and cross-site scripting; blocklists are weak.

flashcards.back: An attack on applications built on large language models in which crafted input, or content the model retrieves, overrides the developer's instructions and causes disclosure or unwanted actions.
flashcards.detail: Defend by treating model output as untrusted, restricting tool permissions, filtering input and output and keeping secrets out of prompts.

flashcards.back: Apply least privilege to model tools and data connectors, validate and sanitize model output before it reaches other systems, log prompts and responses and guard against data leakage and over-reliance on model decisions.
flashcards.detail: Newer outline content; tie it to familiar principles such as input validation, authorization and monitoring.

flashcards.back: Attackers query a deployed model to infer whether specific records were in its training data, reconstruct sensitive attributes or copy the model's behavior.
flashcards.detail: Mitigate with rate limiting, access control, output limits and privacy-preserving training.

flashcards.front: Penetration testing and vulnerability management in the cloud
flashcards.back: Testing needs authorization within the provider's rules of engagement; findings flow into a managed process of prioritizing by risk, remediating and verifying.
flashcards.detail: Never test provider infrastructure without permission; customer-controlled layers are generally allowed within published policy.

flashcards.back: Many small services communicate over the network, so each needs authentication, authorization and encryption; a service mesh can enforce mutual TLS and policy between services.
flashcards.detail: More endpoints mean a larger attack surface; zero trust between services is the cloud-native answer.

flashcards.front: Identity and access management (IAM) for cloud
flashcards.back: The processes and technology for establishing identities, authenticating them, authorizing access to resources and auditing activity, for people and for workloads.
flashcards.detail: Identity is the primary control plane in cloud; most exam scenarios are won by stronger identity, not stronger network.

flashcards.back: Trust between an identity provider and relying services lets users authenticate once and access many systems without separate credentials, with the provider issuing signed assertions or tokens.
flashcards.detail: Federation centralizes authentication and deprovisioning; compromise of the identity provider has broad impact.

flashcards.back: SAML exchanges XML assertions for enterprise web single sign-on; OpenID Connect adds an authentication layer on top of OAuth 2.0 using JSON tokens; OAuth 2.0 delegates authorization to access resources without sharing passwords.
flashcards.detail: OAuth is authorization, not authentication; OpenID Connect is the authentication layer.

flashcards.back: Requiring two or more independent factors: something you know, have or are. Phishing-resistant methods such as hardware security keys and passkeys are strongest.
flashcards.detail: SMS codes are weaker than authenticator apps or hardware keys; privileged and remote access always need MFA.

flashcards.back: RBAC grants permissions through roles tied to job function; ABAC decides using attributes of user, resource and context, allowing finer and more dynamic policy.
flashcards.detail: ABAC scales better for dynamic cloud environments but is harder to audit; RBAC is simpler and common.

flashcards.front: Privileged access management and just-in-time access
flashcards.back: Controls for powerful accounts: vaulting credentials, session recording and granting elevated rights only for a limited approved period.
flashcards.detail: Standing administrator rights are the risk; time-bound elevation shrinks the exposure window.

flashcards.back: Non-human identities that applications and automation use to call services, ideally issued short-lived credentials by the platform instead of long-lived static keys.
flashcards.detail: Leaked static keys are a leading breach cause; prefer role assumption and managed identities.

flashcards.front: Least privilege and separation of duties
flashcards.back: Give each identity only the permissions needed, and split critical tasks so no single person can complete a sensitive action alone.
flashcards.detail: Expect the answer that removes excess entitlements and enforces review of who can approve and who can execute.

flashcards.back: Automated creation, update and removal of accounts across systems (the System for Cross-domain Identity Management standard is common) so access follows joiner, mover and leaver events.
flashcards.detail: Orphaned accounts after departures are a frequent finding; automate deprovisioning.

flashcards.back: A control point between users and cloud services that provides visibility, data protection, threat detection and policy enforcement for sanctioned and unsanctioned services.
flashcards.detail: Answers shadow IT and data-movement scenarios; works through API connections or proxy placement.

flashcards.back: Key sources include management-plane audit logs (who did what through the console and APIs), network flow logs, operating system and application logs, identity provider logs and managed-service logs, all sent to a central protected store.
flashcards.detail: Turn on management-plane logging first; without it you cannot reconstruct an account compromise.

flashcards.back: A platform that collects, normalizes and correlates logs from many sources, raises alerts on suspicious patterns and retains data for investigation and compliance.
flashcards.detail: Correlation and retention are the value; a SIEM fed incomplete or unsynchronized logs gives false comfort.

flashcards.back: Tools that automate repetitive response tasks and orchestrate playbooks across security and IT systems, such as enriching an alert and isolating a host.
flashcards.detail: SIEM detects; SOAR responds. Automate containment of high-confidence, low-impact actions and keep humans in the loop for risky ones.

flashcards.back: Logs should be sent off the system that produced them, protected against tampering, time-synchronized and retained according to legal and investigative needs.
flashcards.detail: Attackers delete local logs first; write-once central storage preserves evidence.

flashcards.back: Continuously checks cloud configurations against benchmarks and policy, flags misconfigurations such as public storage or open management ports and can trigger remediation.
flashcards.detail: Misconfiguration, not exotic exploits, causes most cloud breaches, so CSPM is a staple answer.

flashcards.front: Cloud workload protection and runtime security
flashcards.back: Agent or agentless tooling that monitors running workloads, containers and functions for vulnerabilities, malware and anomalous behavior.
flashcards.detail: Complements posture checks: CSPM looks at configuration, workload protection looks at what is running.

flashcards.back: A baseline is the approved secure configuration; drift is any deviation from it over time, detected automatically and corrected or investigated.
flashcards.detail: Pairs with infrastructure as code: the template is the source of truth, and out-of-band changes are drift.

flashcards.back: A controlled process for requesting, reviewing, approving, testing, implementing and recording changes so they do not introduce unmanaged risk.
flashcards.detail: Emergency changes still need after-the-fact review; unauthorized change is a top cause of outages and incidents.

flashcards.back: Prioritize patches by risk, test, deploy and verify. The customer patches guest operating systems and applications in IaaS; the provider patches the platform layers it operates.
flashcards.detail: Know whose patch it is under each service model; unknown or unowned assets are never patched.

flashcards.back: Reducing attack surface by removing unneeded services, closing ports, applying secure benchmarks and setting strong defaults on every image and instance.
flashcards.detail: Harden the image once and deploy it many times; benchmark checks should be automated.

flashcards.back: Regularly scanning assets, preferably with authenticated scans, then triaging by exploitability and business impact, remediating and verifying the fix.
flashcards.detail: Scanning finds issues; management is the full cycle. Prioritize by risk, not by raw score alone.

flashcards.back: Preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication and recovery; and post-incident learning. NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 aligns incident response with the functions of the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0.
flashcards.detail: Preparation (plans, tooling, contacts, logging) is what makes the other phases possible; containment precedes eradication.

flashcards.back: Ephemeral resources vanish quickly, logs may belong to the provider, responsibilities are split and access to evidence depends on contracts, so customers must prepare in advance with logging, snapshots and provider contacts.
flashcards.detail: Questions reward answers that build capability beforehand rather than improvising mid-incident.

flashcards.back: Limiting the damage by isolating affected resources, for example moving an instance to a quarantine security group, revoking credentials and snapshotting storage, rather than powering it off and destroying volatile evidence.
flashcards.detail: Preserve evidence while stopping spread; revoke or rotate compromised credentials immediately.

flashcards.back: Collecting, preserving and analyzing evidence such as disk snapshots, memory captures and logs in a way that keeps its integrity and admissibility, within the limits of access the provider allows.
flashcards.detail: Work on copies, hash evidence, document everything and know what the provider can supply under contract.

flashcards.back: A documented record of who collected, handled, stored and transferred evidence, with times and purpose, proving it has not been altered.
flashcards.detail: A broken chain of custody can make evidence inadmissible, however good the analysis.

flashcards.back: Collect the most short-lived evidence first: memory and running processes, then network connections, then disk and storage, then remote logs and archival media.
flashcards.detail: In cloud, snapshot memory and volumes before terminating an instance, because the instance may not exist later.

flashcards.back: Preparing in advance to collect evidence quickly: enabling logs, defining retention, setting up isolated analysis accounts, tooling and legal and contractual arrangements with the provider.
flashcards.detail: The cloud equivalent of preparation in the incident life cycle.

flashcards.back: The team and processes that monitor, triage and respond to security events. Useful metrics include mean time to detect and mean time to respond.
flashcards.detail: Measure outcomes over time; alert volume alone says nothing about effectiveness.

flashcards.back: Documented, step-by-step procedures for handling specific incident types or operations, increasingly automated, so response is consistent and fast.
flashcards.detail: Test them in exercises; an untested playbook fails when needed.

flashcards.back: Threat intelligence provides context on adversaries and indicators; threat hunting proactively searches for undetected compromise using hypotheses, and increasingly uses machine learning to find anomalies.
flashcards.detail: Hunting assumes the attacker is already in; the revised outline highlights AI and ML as hunting tools.

flashcards.back: Analytics that build baselines of normal behavior for users and systems and flag deviations, such as impossible travel or unusual data downloads.
flashcards.detail: Useful for detecting stolen credentials and insider abuse where no signature exists.

flashcards.front: Model drift as a security signal
flashcards.back: A deployed machine learning model whose behavior shifts over time without an intentional update may indicate data poisoning, tampering or changed input patterns, so model performance should be monitored like any other control.
flashcards.detail: New AI-related operations content: monitor models for unexpected change and investigate it as a potential incident.

flashcards.front: Intrusion detection and prevention in the cloud
flashcards.back: Network and host based tools, plus provider-native threat detection, that identify and optionally block malicious activity; virtual appliances and traffic mirroring supply the visibility physical taps once gave.
flashcards.detail: Encrypted traffic limits network inspection; host and identity telemetry fill the gap.

flashcards.back: Operations practices from frameworks such as ITIL and ISO/IEC 20000 (incident, problem, change, release, configuration and availability management) feed continual service improvement.
flashcards.detail: Security operations must integrate with these processes, not sit beside them.

flashcards.back: A communication plan names who informs executives, legal counsel, regulators, customers and the provider, with timelines driven by law and contract.
flashcards.detail: Legal and compliance teams decide what is disclosed and when; technical staff do not improvise public statements.

flashcards.back: Operating across several providers requires a normalized log schema, centralized detection, consistent identity and runbooks that account for each provider's tools and evidence limits.
flashcards.detail: A stated emphasis of the newer outline: tool sprawl and inconsistent visibility are the main risks.

flashcards.back: The European Union's privacy regulation governing processing of personal data of people in the EU, with principles of lawfulness, purpose limitation, minimization, accuracy, storage limitation, integrity and confidentiality, and accountability.
flashcards.detail: Applies by whom is affected, not only by where the company sits; fines can reach 4 percent of global annual turnover.

flashcards.back: Individuals can access, correct, erase, restrict, port and object to processing of their personal data, and the controller must be able to honor these requests, including from data held by processors.
flashcards.detail: Design choices such as immutable stores and uncontrolled copies can make rights impossible to meet.

flashcards.back: Residency is where data is physically stored; sovereignty is the principle that data is subject to the laws of the country where it is located or where its controller is based.
flashcards.detail: Cloud replication and support access from other countries can move data across borders unnoticed.

flashcards.back: Personal data may leave the EU only with a lawful mechanism: an adequacy decision, standard contractual clauses, binding corporate rules or a narrow exception, usually backed by a transfer impact assessment.
flashcards.detail: Standard contractual clauses are the most common contract-based tool in cloud agreements.

flashcards.back: Pre-approved contract terms that bind the importer of personal data outside the EU to provide equivalent protection, supplemented by assessment of the destination country's laws.
flashcards.detail: Know when they are needed: transfers to a provider or sub-processor outside an adequate country.

flashcards.back: A structured assessment of privacy risks for processing likely to result in high risk to individuals, such as large-scale profiling or new technologies, carried out before the processing starts.
flashcards.detail: Often required for AI and analytics projects that use personal data at scale.

flashcards.back: Many laws require notifying regulators and sometimes individuals within set deadlines; under GDPR the controller notifies the authority within 72 hours of becoming aware of a reportable breach, and processors must tell the controller without undue delay.
flashcards.detail: The contract with the provider should set how fast the provider tells you.

flashcards.front: Government access and the US CLOUD Act
flashcards.back: The CLOUD Act allows US authorities to compel US-based providers to produce data they control regardless of where it is stored, which can conflict with foreign privacy and sovereignty rules.
flashcards.detail: Customer-held keys and contractual challenge clauses are common mitigations.

flashcards.back: Examples include HIPAA for US health information (with business associate agreements), the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard for card data and Sarbanes-Oxley for financial reporting controls.
flashcards.detail: Match the data type in the scenario to the regime; a processor handling protected health data needs a signed business associate agreement.

flashcards.back: The process of identifying, preserving, collecting, reviewing and producing electronically stored information for litigation or investigation; ISO/IEC 27050 gives guidance.
flashcards.detail: In cloud, ask where data is, how holds are applied, what the provider will produce and who bears the cost.

flashcards.back: Key clauses cover service levels, data ownership and location, security obligations, breach notification, audit and inspection rights, subcontracting, termination and data return and deletion, and liability.
flashcards.detail: The contract is the main tool a customer has to turn provider promises into obligations.

flashcards.back: Because customers rarely audit hyperscale providers directly, they rely on independent audit reports and certifications, and contracts may still reserve inspection rights.
flashcards.detail: Read the scope of any report: it covers only the named services, locations and period.

flashcards.back: SOC 1 addresses controls relevant to financial reporting; SOC 2 reports on security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality and privacy criteria; SOC 3 is a general-use summary. Type I covers design at a point in time, Type II covers operating effectiveness over a period.
flashcards.detail: A Type II SOC 2 is the stronger evidence; check scope, period and exceptions.

flashcards.back: 27001 certifies an information security management system; 27017 adds cloud-specific controls for providers and customers; 27018 covers protection of personal data in public clouds acting as processors.
flashcards.detail: 27001 is certifiable; 27017 and 27018 are guidance and control sets usually assessed alongside it.

flashcards.front: CSA STAR and Cloud Controls Matrix
flashcards.back: The Cloud Security Alliance Cloud Controls Matrix is a framework of cloud security controls; STAR is a public registry in which providers publish assurance, from a self-assessment (Level 1) to third-party audit or certification (Level 2).
flashcards.detail: STAR gives a comparable, vendor-neutral way to review a provider before purchase.

flashcards.front: Risk management process and treatment options
flashcards.back: Identify assets and threats, assess likelihood and impact, then treat the risk by mitigating, transferring (for example insurance or contract), avoiding or accepting it, tracking the rest in a risk register.
flashcards.detail: Risk is accepted by the business owner, not by the security team; cloud adoption transfers some duties but never accountability.

flashcards.back: Appetite is the amount and type of risk an organization is willing to pursue; tolerance is the acceptable variation around objectives.
flashcards.detail: Leadership sets appetite; security recommends controls that keep exposure within it.

flashcards.back: Assess suppliers before onboarding (due diligence), contract for security obligations, monitor performance and evidence continuously and plan for exit, including risks from their own subprocessors.
flashcards.detail: Due diligence is investigation before the decision; due care is acting responsibly afterwards.

flashcards.front: Governance, risk and compliance (GRC) and enterprise risk management
flashcards.back: Governance sets direction and accountability, risk management addresses uncertainty to objectives and compliance demonstrates adherence to laws and policy. ISO 31000 provides a general risk management framework.
flashcards.detail: Cloud risk should feed the enterprise risk register rather than live in a separate silo.

flashcards.front: Shadow IT and its compliance impact
flashcards.back: Staff use unsanctioned cloud services outside IT's visibility, creating unmanaged data flows and compliance gaps.
flashcards.detail: Discover through network and CASB telemetry, then offer approved alternatives rather than only blocking.

flashcards.front: Audit planning and cloud-specific audit challenges
flashcards.back: Define scope, objectives and evidence in advance; cloud adds limited physical access, shared responsibility, dynamic resources and reliance on provider reports, so audits depend on logs, APIs and automation.
flashcards.detail: Continuous control monitoring with automated evidence suits a changing cloud estate.

flashcards.front: Privacy by design and by default
flashcards.back: Building privacy protections into systems from the start and defaulting to the most privacy-protective settings with minimal collection.
flashcards.detail: A GDPR principle; the exam favors answers that embed controls early over bolting them on later.

flashcards.back: Insurance transfers part of the financial impact of an incident but not the legal accountability or the reputational damage, and insurers often require baseline controls.
flashcards.detail: A treatment option, never a substitute for controls.

flashcards.back: A provider may depend on other companies to deliver the service. Customers need visibility of subprocessors, the right to object to changes and flow-down of security and privacy obligations; ISO/IEC 27036 addresses supplier relationships.
flashcards.detail: Under GDPR the processor needs the controller's authorization to engage a subprocessor.

questions.question: A start-up runs a customer relationship management product it licenses from a vendor. The vendor patches the platform; the start-up decides who gets accounts and what data is entered. After a data leak caused by a former employee's still-active account, who holds primary responsibility for that failure?
options: The vendor, because it operates the entire software stack
Neither party, since the account belonged to an individual rather than an organization
The start-up, because user access and data handling stay with the customer in SaaS
Shared equally, because SaaS removes the distinction between the parties
questions.explanation: In SaaS the provider manages the application and below, but customers remain responsible for identity lifecycle, access settings and the data they enter. A stale account is a customer joiner-mover-leaver failure. The vendor's operation of the stack does not extend to deprovisioning the customer's staff, and responsibility is split by layer, not evenly.
questions.whyTested: Tests the part of shared responsibility that never moves, whatever the service model.

questions.question: A team moves a batch-processing application from servers it manages to a managed container platform where the provider operates the host operating system and orchestration. Compared with IaaS, which responsibility has MOST clearly shifted to the provider?
options: Writing and testing the application's authentication logic
Classification and protection of the sensitive data that the application stores and processes on the platform
Defining which staff may deploy new application versions
Patching and hardening of the host operating system and orchestration layer
questions.explanation: Managed platforms move the lower layers (host OS, runtime, orchestration) to the provider. Data classification, application logic and deployment authorization remain with the customer at every service model, which is why they are tempting but wrong.

questions.question: A regional hospital group, a university and a public health agency jointly fund one cloud environment built to a common research-compliance standard and open only to those organizations. Which deployment model is this?
options: Hybrid cloud, because several organizations contribute infrastructure
Private cloud, because access is restricted to named organizations
Community cloud
Multi-cloud, because multiple customers participate
questions.explanation: A community cloud is shared by organizations with a common concern, here the same compliance standard. Private cloud serves one organization. Hybrid joins different deployment models, and multi-cloud means several providers; neither is described.

questions.question: An architect is asked why a workload that scales out automatically at peak and releases servers overnight is described as elastic rather than merely scalable. What is the BEST answer?
options: Capacity is added and removed automatically in response to demand
Resources are shared among tenants to cut cost
The provider guarantees a contractual availability percentage for the service each month
The application can run on larger instance types if needed
questions.explanation: Elasticity is automatic provisioning and release matching demand. A larger instance is vertical scaling by hand, availability guarantees are an SLA matter, and sharing is resource pooling or multi-tenancy.

questions.question: Which statement about the cloud service broker role is MOST accurate?
options: A broker adds value but the customer stays accountable for its own data and compliance
A broker is the independent party that certifies provider controls
A broker replaces the need for a contract with the underlying provider
A broker takes on full legal liability for every item of data that is processed through its platform
questions.explanation: Brokers intermediate, aggregate or add value to services, but accountability for data and compliance cannot be outsourced. Independent certification is the auditor's role, and liability and contracts still need explicit treatment.

questions.question: A security architect must keep the contents of a financial model confidential even from the cloud provider's administrators while the model is being computed on a rented virtual machine. Which technology addresses this requirement BEST?
options: Full-disk encryption with a provider-managed key
TLS 1.3 between the client and the virtual machine
Tokenization of the model's output files
Confidential computing using a hardware-based trusted execution environment
questions.explanation: Confidential computing protects data in use by processing it inside an encrypted, isolated hardware enclave. Disk encryption covers data at rest and, with provider-held keys, does not exclude the provider. TLS covers data in transit, and tokenizing outputs does nothing for the computation itself.
questions.whyTested: Data in use is a growing exam theme and is named in the revised outline.

questions.question: A company wants the freedom to move a critical application to another provider within a few weeks if prices rise. Which design choice BEST supports that goal?
options: Replicate all data to an on-premises server that only IT staff may access
Adopt each provider's proprietary managed database services wherever they improve performance
Build on open standards and containers, keep data portable and document an exit plan
Negotiate a three-year price lock with the incumbent provider
questions.explanation: Portability comes from open standards, portable formats and tested exit procedures. Proprietary services deepen lock-in, a price lock does not create a way out, and a private copy of the data does not make the application portable.

questions.question: Which architectural principle BEST reflects the move from perimeter-based protection to cloud-native security?
options: Allow unrestricted traffic between workloads in the same virtual network
Verify every request using identity, device and context, not network location
Place all workloads inside a single private subnet and rely on its boundary to limit exposure
Rely on the provider's physical security for logical access control
questions.explanation: Zero trust treats identity and context as the control point because there is no trusted network edge in cloud. Flat internal trust and a single subnet recreate the perimeter fallacy, and physical security does not replace logical access control.

questions.question: A team stores purchase records on a managed distributed ledger and later receives a lawful erasure request from a customer. What is the MOST significant design problem this reveals?
options: Ledgers require the provider to hold every participant's private key
Ledgers cannot be replicated across regions for resilience
Ledgers cannot be encrypted when the data is at rest
Immutable ledger entries cannot be removed, which conflicts with deletion obligations for personal data
questions.explanation: Immutability is a feature for integrity and a defect for erasure rights, so personal data should stay off-chain with only references or hashes on it. Ledgers can be encrypted and replicated, and participants keep their own keys.

questions.question: Why is the roadmap for post-quantum cryptography a concern today for data that must remain confidential for twenty years?
options: Quantum computers will make all symmetric hashing completely unusable as soon as they exist
Adversaries can collect encrypted traffic now and decrypt it once quantum capability exists
Quantum computing can erase data from encrypted storage remotely
Cloud providers will stop supporting current TLS versions this year
questions.explanation: Harvest-now, decrypt-later makes long-lived secrets vulnerable well before capable quantum computers arrive, motivating crypto agility and migration planning. The other statements overstate or invent effects.

questions.question: A customer asks which document tells them how much downtime the provider will tolerate before credits are owed. Which is the BEST answer?
options: The shared responsibility matrix
The service level agreement
The provider's SOC 2 report
The data processing addendum
questions.explanation: The SLA states measurable service targets and remedies. A SOC 2 report describes controls, the responsibility matrix divides security duties, and a data processing addendum covers personal data handling.

questions.question: An IoT fleet sends telemetry to a cloud ingestion service. Which design decision MOST reduces the risk of a stolen device injecting false data?
options: Use a shared API key embedded in the firmware of all devices
Accept data from any source address in the manufacturer's range
Encrypt telemetry with a single key that is stored in each device's clear-text configuration file
Give each device a unique certificate-based identity and authenticate every connection
questions.explanation: Per-device identities allow revocation of one compromised unit without disrupting the fleet. A shared key is exposed by one extracted device, IP ranges are spoofable and a clear-text key offers no protection.

questions.question: Which activity is MOST clearly the cloud customer's responsibility regardless of the service model?
options: Deciding who may access their data and how it is classified
Maintaining the hypervisor and host firmware
Replacing failed disks in the provider's storage arrays
Controlling physical access to the provider's data centers
questions.explanation: Data governance and access decisions always rest with the customer. Hypervisors, data-center access and hardware maintenance are provider duties in all service models.

questions.question: An architect reviews a design against ISO/IEC 17789 cross-cutting aspects and finds no plan for leaving the provider. Which aspect has been overlooked?
options: Maintenance and versioning
Reversibility
Elasticity
Performance
questions.explanation: Reversibility concerns retrieving customer assets and having remaining copies deleted on exit. Elasticity, maintenance and performance are separate aspects and do not address exit.

questions.question: A data science team wants to fine-tune a hosted foundation model with customer support transcripts. Under shared responsibility, which duty stays with the customer?
options: Classifying and protecting the training data and access to the tuned model
Operating the provider's model-serving network
Securing the physical GPU servers that run the training job
Patching the underlying operating system of the managed training service's hosts
questions.explanation: Even on a fully managed AI service, the training data, access to the resulting model and the choice of what to feed it belong to the customer. Hardware, platform patching and provider networking are provider duties.
questions.whyTested: The revised outline integrates AI and ML into each domain, so shared responsibility for AI services is fair game.

questions.question: Which TWO characteristics distinguish a true cloud service from ordinary hosted infrastructure? (Choose two.)
options: The customer owns the physical servers
Workloads cannot move between regions
Customers can provision resources on demand without human interaction
Usage is metered so it can be measured and billed
Capacity is fixed in a multi-year contract
questions.explanation: On-demand self-service and measured service are NIST essential characteristics. Fixed capacity contracts and customer-owned hardware are traits of traditional hosting, and cloud workloads commonly can move between regions.

questions.question: Which TWO statements about multi-cloud strategies are accurate? (Choose two.)
options: They guarantee workload portability without any code change
They can reduce dependence on one provider and improve resilience
They remove the need for a shared responsibility analysis
They are identical to hybrid cloud by definition
They increase the work needed for consistent identity, logging and policy
questions.explanation: Using several providers spreads risk but multiplies operational and governance complexity. Each provider still needs a responsibility analysis, portability is never automatic and hybrid cloud is a different concept.

questions.question: Which THREE items are properly the provider's responsibility in an IaaS deployment? (Choose three.)
options: Guest operating system patching
Hypervisor and host patching
Availability of the underlying storage service
Physical data-center security
Firewall rules for customer virtual networks
questions.explanation: Facilities, hypervisor and core service availability belong to the provider. In IaaS the customer patches guest operating systems and configures their own network controls.

questions.question: Which TWO technologies are most directly aimed at limiting exposure of data while it is being processed? (Choose two.)
options: Full-disk encryption
Transport Layer Security
Confidential computing with trusted execution environments
Homomorphic or secure multi-party computation techniques
Hash-based message authentication
questions.explanation: Both enclaves and privacy-preserving computation protect data in use. TLS and disk encryption cover transit and rest, and message authentication provides integrity of messages rather than confidentiality of processing.

questions.question: Which TWO risks are especially associated with edge computing deployments? (Choose two.)
options: Inability to use encryption on any link
Many physically accessible nodes that attackers can tamper with
Complete reliance on a single central data center
Inconsistent patching across a widely distributed fleet
questions.explanation: Edge widens the physical and patching surface. It reduces dependence on one center and can use encryption normally.

questions.question: In a SaaS model the customer is relieved of all accountability for data protection because the provider operates the application.
questions.explanation: The provider operates the application stack, but the customer remains accountable for its data, user access and configuration choices.

questions.question: A hybrid cloud always involves two or more different cloud providers.
questions.explanation: Hybrid means distinct deployment models, typically private and public, bound together. Two public providers is multi-cloud.

questions.question: Measured service means the provider monitors resource use so it can be reported, controlled and billed.
questions.explanation: Metering underlies pay-per-use billing, quotas and cost anomaly detection.

questions.question: Multi-tenancy is a risk the customer can eliminate by choosing any reputable provider.
questions.explanation: It is inherent to pooled cloud resources; customers manage the risk through isolation choices, encryption and dedicated options, not by eliminating it.

questions.question: Containers and serverless functions are examples of technologies the CCSP treats as part of the cloud reference architecture's impact of related technologies.
questions.explanation: The outline asks you to consider how containers, edge, confidential computing, AI and similar technologies affect architecture and security.

questions.question: Reversibility means the customer can retrieve their data and have the provider delete the remaining copies when the relationship ends.
questions.explanation: It is one of the cross-cutting aspects and should be backed by contract terms and verified deletion.

questions.question: Moving a workload from IaaS to PaaS leaves the customer's responsibilities exactly unchanged.
questions.explanation: Operating system and runtime duties move to the provider; application, identity and data duties remain.

questions.question: Data in use can be protected using trusted execution environments built into the processor.
questions.explanation: Hardware enclaves isolate and encrypt memory during computation, which is the aim of confidential computing.

questions.question: A cloud customer must prove to an auditor that a decommissioned database is unrecoverable, but cannot access the provider's physical disks. Which approach is MOST appropriate?
options: Ask the provider to confirm it will degauss the disks eventually
Move the database to another region and delete the first copy
Overwrite the logical volume once with zeros before releasing it
Encrypt the data with customer-controlled keys and destroy all copies of the keys
questions.explanation: Cryptographic erasure is the accepted cloud answer because customers cannot physically sanitize shared media. A single logical overwrite may not touch all replicas, a promise to degauss is unverifiable and moving regions just leaves more copies.
questions.whyTested: Sanitization in cloud is a signature CCSP topic; the exam expects crypto-shredding.

questions.question: A company learns that its object storage contains several unknown buckets with customer records. What should the security architect do FIRST to bring the data under control?
options: Deploy DLP policies that block all uploads to cloud storage
Run data discovery to find and inventory where sensitive data is stored
Ask the data custodian to delete all unknown buckets
Apply the strictest encryption setting to every bucket in the account immediately
questions.explanation: You cannot classify, encrypt or govern data you have not located; discovery comes first. Blanket encryption and blocking are premature, and deleting unknown buckets risks destroying data under legal hold or business need.

questions.question: A law firm sends a confidential contract to an external party and must be able to revoke that party's access after the project ends, even if the file has been downloaded. Which control BEST meets this requirement?
options: Transport Layer Security on the file transfer
Full-disk encryption on the sender's laptop
Data loss prevention rules on the outbound email gateway and web proxy
Information rights management applied to the document
questions.explanation: IRM is persistent protection that follows the file and can be revoked. DLP only gates egress, TLS protects the transfer in transit and disk encryption protects one device.

questions.question: A developer wants realistic customer data in a test environment, but the test team does not need real identities. Which approach MOST reduces risk?
options: Apply irreversible static masking before copying data to the test environment
Encrypt the production copy with the same key as production
Tokenize the data and share the vault with the test team
Copy production data into the test environment and restrict access to the test team only
questions.explanation: Irreversible masking removes real values so a test breach exposes nothing. Restricting access still leaves real data in a weaker environment, sharing the token vault defeats the point and reusing the production key enlarges exposure.

questions.question: Under privacy law, which statement about pseudonymized data is MOST accurate?
options: It no longer requires a lawful basis for processing
It is anonymous and falls outside privacy regulation
It remains personal data because the separate mapping allows re-identification
It can be freely shared with any third party
questions.explanation: Pseudonymization is a safeguard, not an exemption: if re-identification is possible with additional information, the data is still regulated. Only effective anonymization removes it from scope.

questions.question: A regulation requires records to be kept for seven years, yet a pending lawsuit concerns some of those records. A lifecycle rule would delete anything older than three years. What should the architect do?
options: Let the three-year rule run and restore from backups if needed
Delete the records to reduce eDiscovery exposure
Suspend deletion for the affected records under a legal hold and align the retention rule to the longest applicable requirement
Move the records to a cheaper storage tier and keep the existing three-year deletion rule running unchanged
questions.explanation: Legal and regulatory retention outrank convenient lifecycle rules; a legal hold must prevent destruction. Deleting relevant records can be spoliation, relying on backups is unreliable and tiering does not stop deletion.

questions.question: Who is accountable for deciding the classification of a dataset hosted in a public cloud?
options: The cloud provider's security team
The database administrator who runs the service
The cloud service broker
The data owner within the customer organization
questions.explanation: The owner determines classification and access; custodians and providers implement. Accountability for data is never transferred through custody or brokerage.

questions.question: A bank wants to stop employees from uploading files containing account numbers to personal cloud storage, including over encrypted connections. Which solution is MOST suitable?
options: Encrypting every file with a shared team password
A firewall rule blocking all outbound traffic on port 443 for every employee workstation
A cloud access security broker or DLP control that can inspect the content
A policy memo reminding staff of acceptable use
questions.explanation: Content-aware DLP at a point that can decrypt or see activity addresses the requirement. Blocking port 443 breaks the business, a shared password is weak and does not prevent upload, and a memo is not a technical control.

questions.question: A data science team is building a model from several public and internal sources. Which data security concern is MOST specific to this scenario?
options: The model's training job runs inside a private virtual network with restricted egress
The dataset is stored as compressed files
The team uses a notebook to explore the data
Poisoned or tampered training data silently degrading the model's integrity
questions.explanation: Integrity and provenance of training data are the particular risk, since poisoned inputs corrupt every resulting model. Network placement, compression and notebooks are ordinary engineering choices without the same specific risk.
questions.whyTested: New AI content in the revised outline is woven into data security.

questions.question: In most cloud scenarios involving personal data, how are the customer and provider classified?
options: Both as joint data subjects
Provider as data owner and customer as custodian
Customer as processor and provider as controller
Customer as controller and provider as processor
questions.explanation: The customer decides purposes and means and so is controller; the provider processes on its instructions. The reverse is wrong unless the provider uses the data for its own purposes.

questions.question: Why does erasure coding across several locations improve a cloud storage system's durability?
options: Data is split into fragments with redundancy so lost fragments can be rebuilt
The provider mirrors all data into the customer's data center
Data is encrypted using a different key for each fragment
Every copy of the data is stored in full in every region that the provider operates worldwide
questions.explanation: Dispersion with redundancy lets the system reconstruct data after partial loss. Full copies everywhere is replication, per-fragment keys are unrelated and mirroring to the customer is not how it works.

questions.question: A security team can see a sudden volume of queries from a privileged database administrator reading many customer rows at night. Which control would have given the BEST independent evidence of this activity?
options: A stricter password and rotation policy for all database administrators
Encryption of the database volume
